context: factory · spinning, weaving / knitting, dyeing & finishing; humidity control and effluent treatment

brief.intro: New to this project type? A textile mill can cover one or all of the steps from fibre to fabric. Spinning opens and cleans the fibre, cards and draws it and spins it into yarn. Weaving or knitting turns yarn into fabric on hundreds of looms or knitting machines. Dyeing and finishing — the 'wet' part — bleaches, dyes, prints and finishes the fabric using steam, hot water and chemicals. The spinning and weaving halls are large, windowless and air-conditioned to a constant humidity, because the yarn breaks if the air is too dry; under the floor run ducts that carry waste fibre and return air. The wet-processing section needs boilers, a great deal of water and an effluent treatment plant, which the environmental permit will insist on.

must_get_right: Under-floor trenches and ducts for return air and waste must be built with the floor — the machine layout must be frozen before the slab.
Humidity must be under control before the machines run; plan the humidification plant ahead of the machinery trials.
The effluent treatment plant and its discharge permit gate the dye house — start them with the main works, not at the end.
Hundreds of similar machines are erected by the supplier's fitters in a fixed sequence; the building must be dust-free and powered before they start.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Layout freeze → foundations and floor with trenches → building enclosed → humidification plant and power → machinery erection by section → trials → quality. The dye house follows its own chain: boilers, water and effluent plant → machines → colour trials. The critical path runs through machinery delivery, or through the effluent plant and permit for the wet section.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: layout changes after the floor is cast, late machinery, humidity not achieved, effluent permit, and skilled-operator shortage during ramp-up. Contingency is held before first saleable production.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
